name: Retina to visual cortex

steps.label: Retinal ganglion cells
steps.note: Axons carry retinal output; retinal surface is not separately modeled.

steps.label: Optic chiasm
steps.note: Nasal retinal fibres cross; temporal retinal fibres remain ipsilateral.

steps.label: Optic tract
steps.note: Each tract represents the contralateral visual hemifield from both eyes.

steps.label: Optic radiation
steps.note: Temporal Meyer's loop carries superior-field information; parietal route carries inferior-field information.

steps.label: Extrastriate processing
steps.note: V2 is one of several extrastriate areas; streams are interconnected rather than two isolated pipelines.

clinical: Unilateral postchiasmal injury may cause contralateral homonymous field loss; pattern depends on lesion extent. Macular sparing can occur in occipital infarction but is not obligatory.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), pp. 463-476 (PDF pp. 489-502), Figures 11.6-11.8 and 11.15
summary: Retina to visual cortex — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Ascending auditory network

steps.label: Cochlear nuclei
steps.note: Dorsal cochlear nucleus also contributes; the diagram is a branched network, not one obligatory serial route.

steps.label: Superior olivary complex
steps.note: Receives bilateral input via crossing and uncrossed projections; some cochlear projections bypass it.

steps.label: Lateral lemniscus
steps.note: Auditory information ascends bilaterally with contralateral predominance.

steps.label: Auditory radiation
steps.note: Separate tract mesh unavailable; passes through sublenticular internal capsule.

clinical: A unilateral lesion above the cochlear nuclei usually does not cause complete unilateral deafness. Bilateral central injury can impair hearing or auditory recognition.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 519-522 (PDF pp. 545-548), Figures 12.16-12.17
summary: Ascending auditory network — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Hippocampal intrinsic memory circuit

steps.label: Perforant pathway
steps.note: Input to dentate/CA3 arises predominantly from superficial layer II; a mainly layer III input to CA1 forms a parallel route. Other layer contributions occur. The cited laminar tracing evidence is from macaque, not a measured human atlas connection.

steps.label: Mossy fibres
steps.note: Axons of dentate granule cells.

steps.label: CA3
steps.note: Grouped CA2/CA3 atlas record is a display convenience; CA2 is not a compulsory relay of the trisynaptic route.

clinical: Medial temporal damage may impair formation of new declarative memories; outcome depends on bilateral extent and wider memory networks.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 834-837 (PDF pp. 860-863), Figures 18.8, 18.11 and 18.13

Witter MP, Amaral DG (1991). Entorhinal cortex of the monkey: V. Projections to dentate gyrus, hippocampus, and subicular complex. J Comp Neurol 307:437-459. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1713237/ (primary macaque tracing; layer contributions are preferential, not exclusive)
summary: Hippocampal intrinsic memory circuit — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Papez memory circuit (simplified)

steps.label: Mammillothalamic tract
steps.note: Not separately modeled.

clinical: Fornical, mammillary or anterior thalamic injury can disrupt memory. This heuristic omits direct fornix-to-anterior-thalamus and many other reciprocal pathways; it is not an isolated emotion circuit.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 834-837 (PDF pp. 860-863), Figures 18.8, 18.11 and 18.13
summary: Papez memory circuit (simplified) — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Basal ganglia direct pathway (teaching model)

steps.label: Motor/premotor cortex
steps.note: Glutamatergic excitation of striatum.

steps.label: Striatal direct-pathway neurons
steps.note: GABAergic inhibition of GPi/SNr; dopamine generally facilitates D1-expressing neurons in this model.

steps.label: GPi/SNr output
steps.note: Reduced tonic inhibition can disinhibit motor thalamus; SNr is a parallel output nucleus.

clinical: The rate model helps explain movement selection but does not account for all firing patterns, tremor, dystonia or DBS effects.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 748-752 (PDF pp. 774-778), Figures 16.5-16.8; textbook explicitly describes direct/indirect model as incomplete
summary: Basal ganglia direct pathway (teaching model) — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Basal ganglia indirect pathway (teaching model)

steps.label: Motor/premotor cortex
steps.note: Excites striatal neurons.

steps.label: Striatal indirect-pathway neurons
steps.note: GABAergic inhibition of GPe; dopamine generally reduces D2-pathway activity in this model.

steps.label: GPe
steps.note: Reduced GPe inhibition disinhibits STN.

steps.label: STN
steps.note: Excites GPi/SNr.

steps.label: GPi/SNr
steps.note: Inhibits motor thalamus.

clinical: Classical net effect suppresses competing actions; hyperdirect cortex-to-STN input and recurrent GPe-STN circuitry also contribute and are omitted here.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 748-752 (PDF pp. 774-778), Figures 16.5-16.8; textbook explicitly describes direct/indirect model as incomplete
summary: Basal ganglia indirect pathway (teaching model) — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Dominant perisylvian language network

steps.label: Dorsal language connections (arcuate-related)
steps.note: Arcuate/SLF-related dorsal routes contribute to auditory-motor integration and repetition. Parallel ventral temporal-frontal connections also contribute to comprehension and are not represented by the arcuate link. Naming conventions vary; the arcuate is not the entire SLF.

clinical: Left hemisphere is language dominant in most people, not all. Aphasia patterns depend on distributed cortical/subcortical damage, and the route is reciprocal rather than a single serial chain.
refs: Blumenfeld, 2nd ed., pp. 885-887 and 894-897 (PDF pp. 911-913 and 920-923), Figure 19.2; language processing involves distributed reciprocal networks
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2584675/
summary: Dominant perisylvian language network — major connections in a simplified teaching route.
organization: Connections may be parallel, reciprocal or recurrent. The numbered sequence is a teaching aid, not an obligatory chain or a traced 3D streamline.

name: Voluntary limb motor output
summary: Cortex to spinal motor circuits for skilled limb movement.
organization: Axons descend before synapsing in spinal circuits; most cross in the caudal medulla. The spinal and peripheral portions are not fully modeled.

steps.label: Basis pedunculi and ventral pontine fascicles
Pyramidal decussation
steps.note: Most corticospinal axons cross here; crossing proportions vary.

steps.label: Spinal interneurons and anterior horn motor neurons
Peripheral motor axons and limb muscles

clinical: A lesion above pyramidal crossing usually causes contralateral limb weakness; a spinal lesion affects the ipsilateral side below its level. Acute lesions may initially lack spasticity.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 6, pp. 231-242, Figures 6.8-6.11

name: Voluntary orofacial motor output
summary: Cortical motor networks to cranial motor nuclei and orofacial muscles.
organization: Predominantly bilateral projections, with important contralateral lower-face/genioglossus components. Gaze commands use additional supranuclear networks.

steps.label: Cranial motor nerves and target muscles

clinical: Unilateral supranuclear injury often weakens the opposite lower face; bilateral injury may cause pseudobulbar dysarthria/dysphagia. No single crossing describes all cranial targets.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, pp. 512-514, 535-538, Figure 12.7 and clinical concepts

name: Body discriminative touch and proprioception
summary: Body vibration, position sense and fine touch to somatosensory cortex.
organization: First-order fibres ascend on the same side; second-order fibres cross in the caudal medulla. Face information follows a different trigeminal route.

steps.label: Internal arcuate sensory decussation
steps.note: Crossing in caudal medulla, distinct from pyramidal motor crossing.

clinical: Spinal posterior-column injury causes ipsilateral sensory loss below the lesion; medial-lemniscal injury causes contralateral body loss.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, pp. 277-280, Figures 7.1 and 7.3

name: Body pain and temperature
summary: Ascending nociceptive/thermal information with sensory, affective and arousal branches.
organization: Crossing usually occurs within one or a few spinal segments; multiple thalamic/brainstem routes process pain in parallel.

steps.label: Nociceptors/thermal receptors and dorsal root ganglia
Dorsal horn relay
steps.note: Afferents may ascend/descend briefly in Lissauer tract.

steps.label: Spinal anterior white commissure
steps.note: Most second-order fibres cross.

steps.label: VPL and additional medial/intralaminar thalamic relays
Somatosensory, insular and cingulate cortical networks

clinical: Hemicord injury may cause contralateral pain/temperature loss starting below the lesion; central cord injury can affect crossing fibres bilaterally.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, pp. 278-282, Figures 7.2 and 7.4

name: Facial and oral somatosensation
summary: Touch and pain/temperature from trigeminal territories to thalamocortical circuits.
organization: Touch relays mainly in principal nucleus; pain/temperature relays in spinal trigeminal nucleus. Most ascending fibres cross, with a smaller uncrossed oral tactile route.

steps.label: Principal sensory or spinal trigeminal nuclear relay

clinical: Lateral brainstem injury often combines ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss (pre-crossing spinal trigeminal damage) with contralateral body loss. Crossed ascending pathway injury can instead affect the opposite face.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, pp. 509-512, Figure 12.8

name: Horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex
summary: Stabilizes gaze during head rotation through vestibular and ocular motor circuits.
organization: Example: leftward head rotation activates left horizontal canal circuitry, exciting right abducens/lateral rectus and left medial rectus while inhibiting antagonists. This is one of several VOR circuits.

steps.label: Contralateral medial rectus neurons of CN III
Cerebellar calibration
steps.note: Floccular circuits modify VOR gain; not an obligatory serial output relay.

clinical: Peripheral and central vestibular lesions can disturb gaze stability. MLF lesions may cause ipsilateral adduction impairment in INO.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, pp. 523-525, Figure 12.19
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, pp. 584-587, Figure 13.13

name: Corticopontocerebellar input
summary: Cortical information reaches the opposite cerebellar hemisphere through pontine relays.
organization: Corticopontine fibres terminate in ipsilateral pons; a different neuron population crosses as pontocerebellar fibres.
clinical: Supratentorial and pontine lesions can produce network ataxia. The expected side differs before versus after the pontocerebellar crossing.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, pp. 704-710, Figures 15.9-15.10

name: Spinocerebellar feedback
summary: Parallel sensory and spinal-interneuronal feedback pathways for coordination.
organization: Dorsal/cuneocerebellar routes mainly remain ipsilateral; the ventral route predominantly crosses in cord and recrosses in cerebellum. These are branches, not consecutive relays.

steps.label: Dorsal spinocerebellar branch via Clarke column
Ventral spinocerebellar branch
steps.note: Crosses in cord; enters superior peduncle and predominantly recrosses on entering/within cerebellum, not at cerebellar output decussation.

steps.label: Upper-limb cuneocerebellar and rostral spinocerebellar branches
steps.note: Separate route geometries not modeled.

clinical: Cerebellar and spinocerebellar injury generally produces ipsilateral limb incoordination. Associated conscious sensory loss requires other pathways.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, pp. 708-711, Table 15.3 and Figure 15.11

name: Cerebellar motor feedback
summary: Cerebellar cortex/deep nuclei influence cortical and brainstem motor systems.
organization: Purkinje neurons inhibit deep nuclei; excitatory output from dentate/interposed chiefly crosses through superior peduncle. Fastigial/vestibular routes include bilateral outputs.

steps.label: Descending motor pathways cross again
steps.note: Net cerebellar relationship to limb coordination is principally ipsilateral. Parallel fastigial-to-vestibular/reticular outputs are omitted.

clinical: Lesions before SCP output crossing usually impair the ipsilateral limb; lesions of crossed outputs can cause ataxia contralateral to the brainstem lesion.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, pp. 704-708, Figures 15.9A-C

name: Basal ganglia hyperdirect route
summary: Rapid cortex-to-STN input to basal ganglia output networks.
organization: Simplified excitatory cortex→STN→GPi/SNr route, converging with direct/indirect circuits; firing dynamics exceed a simple rate model.

steps.label: Subthalamic nucleus
steps.note: Excitatory cortical input.

steps.label: GPi/SNr output
steps.note: Excitatory STN input; output nuclei inhibit thalamic/brainstem targets.

clinical: Provides a teaching model of action control; it is not a complete mechanism for tremor, dystonia or deep brain stimulation.
refs: Nambu et al. (2000), Excitatory cortical inputs to pallidal neurons via the subthalamic nucleus in the monkey, J Neurophysiol 84:289-300, https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.2000.84.1.289 (primary primate physiology; not a full model of human behavior)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, pp. 748-752 (context and limitations of direct/indirect model)

name: Descending oculosympathetic pathway
summary: Three-neuron sympathetic route to pupillary dilation and eyelid smooth muscle.
organization: Central descent is mainly ipsilateral; spinal preganglionic axons relay in superior cervical ganglion before postganglionic fibres reach eye.

steps.label: Sympathetic chain and superior cervical ganglion
Iris dilator and eyelid smooth muscle

clinical: Interruption at central, preganglionic or postganglionic levels may cause ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The symptom alone does not establish the level or cause.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, pp. 578-581, Figure 13.10

name: Visceral sensory and vagal reflex network
summary: Visceral afferents connect medullary autonomic circuits with parasympathetic output.
organization: Distributed parallel circuits include NTS, dorsal vagal/ambiguus outputs and respiratory/reticular/hypothalamic networks.

steps.label: Solitary nucleus relay
steps.note: Medullary sensory integration; relay not necessarily the same group as taste neurons.

steps.label: Dorsal vagal and cardiac ambiguus output circuits

clinical: Medullary or vagal lesions may affect autonomic function; dysphagia/dysphonia mainly involve branchial motor pathways rather than dorsal vagal motor neurons alone.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, pp. 530-535, Figures 12.22-12.23
